*Write-up* (Report) can be found at `Questions/Question1/Question1.pdf`


## Data

I only load the data I ended up using for this question.

```{r Q1_data}
Idx_Daily  <- read_rds("Questions/Question1/data/Index_Returns_Daily.rds")
MSCI <- read_rds("Questions/Question1/data/MSCI_Indexes.rds")
Uncertainty <- read_rds("Questions/Question1/data/Econ_Uncertainty_Indexes.rds")
SafeCore <- read_rds("Questions/Question1/data/SafeCore.rds")
Stocks <- read_rds("Questions/Question1/data/Stock_Returns_Daily.rds")
Cons <- read_rds("Questions/Question1/data/Index_Constituents.rds")
Factor_Scores <- read_rds("Questions/Question1/data/Factor_Scores.rds")
```

## Part A 

My first thought was that Part A can really be further divided into two parts. These parts are whether volatility has gone up, and whether it moves with offshore markets. So I needed both local and global series on the same footing. 

For the local market I used the Capped SWIX (J433), since it is the broad market index and also SafeCore's benchmark. I added the Mid Cap (J201) and Small Cap (J202) indices because I wanted to see whether any increase was only in the large companies or across the whole market. For global markets I used MSCI World (developed markets) and MSCI Emerging Markets, since South Africa is usually grouped with emerging markets. I first converted the MSCI data to daily returns (since it is in levels) and I started everything in 2015 because that is where the local data starts.

```{r Q1_A_Rets}
Local_Rets <-
  Idx_Daily %>%
  filter(Tickers %in% c("J433", "J201", "J202"))

Global_Rets <-
  MSCI %>%
  filter(Ticker %in% c("MXWO Index", "MXEF Index")) %>%
  Q1_Level_to_Returns() %>%
  filter(date >= ymd(20150101))

Eq_Rets <- bind_rows(Local_Rets, Global_Rets)
```

I started with a rolling standard deviation to see how volatility changes through time. I chose a 63 day window (about three months) because it matches the three month horizon of the currency volatility index in the data (it is also not too noisy). I annualised it with the square root of 252 as is standard practice. I split the plot into local and global panels so the two groups are easy to compare.

```{r Q1_A_RollVol}
Roll_Vol <- Eq_Rets %>% Rolling_Vol(Window = 63)

g_roll <- Roll_Vol %>%
  mutate(Region = ifelse(Tickers %in% c("J433", "J201", "J202"), "Local", "Global")) %>%
  ggplot() +
  geom_line(aes(date, RollSD, color = Name), alpha = 0.8) +
  facet_wrap(~Region, ncol = 1) +
  labs(title = "Rolling Volatility: Local vs Global Equity",
       subtitle = "63 day rolling standard deviation, annualised",
       x = "", y = "Annualised SD") +
  fmxdat::theme_fmx()

fmxdat::finplot(g_roll, y.pct = T, y.pct_acc = 1)
```

Local and global volatility both have their largest increases at the same time, which suggests that local markets are affected by shocks that start offshore. However, it is difficult to see from this plot whether volatility has increased over time, so I also summarised volatility per calendar year.

```{r Q1_A_AnnVol}
Annual_Vol <- Eq_Rets %>%
  mutate(Year = format(date, "%Y")) %>%
  group_by(Name, Year) %>%
  summarise(SD = sd(Returns, na.rm = T) * sqrt(252)) %>% ungroup()

g_ann <- Annual_Vol %>%
  ggplot() +
  geom_bar(aes(Year, SD, fill = Name), stat = "identity", position = "dodge") +
  labs(title = "Realised Volatility by Calendar Year", x = "Year", y = "Annualised SD") +
  fmxdat::theme_fmx() + fmxdat::fmx_fills()

fmxdat::finplot(g_ann, y.pct = T, y.pct_acc = 1, x.vert = T)
```

Local volatility has not increased over the whole sample, but is high in certain periods, with clear peaks in 2020, 2022 and 2026. Local volatility is also higher than MSCI World in almost every year and closer to MSCI Emerging Markets.

A limitation of the rolling standard deviation is that one extreme day affects the whole window. I wanted to check that the pattern still holds once the noise is removed, so I fitted a GARCH model to the Capped SWIX and MSCI World. I used a GJR-GARCH rather than a standard GARCH, because the standard model treats positive and negative shocks the same, while in stock markets negative returns tend to raise volatility by more. I fitted the two indices separately using `group_split` and `map`, and cached the chunk since it takes a while to run.

```{r Q1_A_Garch, cache = TRUE}
Garch_Out <-
  Eq_Rets %>%
  filter(Tickers %in% c("J433", "MXWO Index")) %>%
  filter(!is.na(Returns)) %>%
  group_split(Tickers) %>%
  map(~Q1_Garch_Sigma(.))

g_garch <-
  Garch_Out %>% map_df(~.$Sigma) %>%
  ggplot() +
  geom_line(aes(date, sigma, color = Tickers), alpha = 0.8) +
  labs(title = "GJR-GARCH Conditional Volatility", subtitle = "Capped SWIX vs MSCI World (Annualised Sigma)",
       x = "Year", y = "Annualised sigma") +
  fmxdat::theme_fmx()

fmxdat::finplot(g_garch, y.pct = T, y.pct_acc = 1)

# Coefficient tables
Garch_Out[[1]]$Coefs
Garch_Out[[2]]$Coefs
```

The large increases in global volatility line up with increases in local volatility, which suggests that local markets follow global markets during periods of stress. For both indices, alpha1 is close to zero while gamma1 is large, although the p-values of a GARCH fit should not be interpreted too strictly. Therefore, volatility increases mainly after negative returns. Persistence is close to one for both, so once volatility increases it takes a long time to settle.

## Part B

TThe question asks whether SafeCore navigates volatility effectively, what the main sources of its volatility are and what its factor exposures are, so I looked at each of these in turn.

SafeCore only gives monthly holdings, so I first had to build its daily returns by applying the monthly weights to the daily stock returns (using `Safe_Return.portfolio`). I used the Capped SWIX as the benchmark throughout (as the question specifies). I started with cumulative returns to get an overall picture.

```{r Q1_B_Rets}
SafeCore_Rets <- Q1_SafeCore_Returns(Holdings = SafeCore, Stocks = Stocks)

BM_Rets <- Idx_Daily %>% filter(Tickers == "J433", date >= min(SafeCore_Rets$date))

g_cum <-
  bind_rows(SafeCore_Rets, BM_Rets) %>%
  arrange(date) %>%
  group_by(Name) %>%
  mutate(CP = cumprod(1 + Returns)) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  ggplot() +
  geom_line(aes(date, CP, color = Name)) +
  labs(title = "Cumulative Returns", subtitle = "SafeCore vs Capped SWIX (J433)", x = "Year", y = "Growth of R1") +
  fmxdat::theme_fmx()

fmxdat::finplot(g_cum)
```

SafeCore clearly outperformed! But, alas, the question is about volatility. Thus, I needed risk measures as well. I used the general financial stats table function, which I set up once in the root `code/` folder so I can reuse it. It needs monthly returns, so I converted the daily returns to monthly first. I looked at the last 3 and 5 years to focus on how the fund has behaved recently.

```{r Q1_B_Stats}
Monthly_Rets <-
  bind_rows(SafeCore_Rets, BM_Rets) %>%
  arrange(date) %>%
  group_by(Tickers) %>%
  mutate(Index = cumprod(1 + Returns)) %>%
  mutate(Yearmonth = format(date, "%Y%B")) %>%
  group_by(Tickers, Yearmonth) %>%
  filter(date == last(date)) %>%
  group_by(Tickers) %>%
  mutate(Ret = Index / lag(Index) - 1) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  filter(!is.na(Ret)) %>%
  select(date, Tickers, Ret)

Tab_stats <-
  bind_rows(
    Moments_Comp(Monthly_Rets, BM = "J433", Yrs_LookBack = 3, NA_Check = 0.8),
    Moments_Comp(Monthly_Rets, BM = "J433", Yrs_LookBack = 5, NA_Check = 0.8)
  )

Tab_stats
```

Over the last three and five years, SafeCore outperformed its benchmark, but with higher volatility and deeper average drawdowns. Its bear beta is below one, which suggests that SafeCore falls by less than its benchmark in a typical down month. When volatility rises, the losses are what matter most, so I also looked at downside risk measures over the full period. 

```{r Q1_B_Downside}
tabdownside <-
  table.DownsideRisk(left_join(SafeCore_Rets %>% select(date, SafeCore = Returns),
                               BM_Rets %>% select(date, J433 = Returns),
                               by = "date") %>% tbl_xts(.),
                     ci = 0.95, Rf = 0, MAR = 0)

tabdownside[c(1,5,7,8:11),]

DD <-
  bind_rows(SafeCore_Rets, BM_Rets) %>%
  arrange(date) %>%
  group_by(Name) %>%
  mutate(CP = cumprod(1 + Returns)) %>%
  mutate(Drawdown = CP / cummax(CP) - 1) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  select(date, Name, Drawdown) %>%
  spread(Name, Drawdown) %>%
  mutate(Diff = SafeCore - `Capped SWIX`) %>%
  filter(!is.na(Diff))

g_dd <-
  DD %>%
  ggplot() +
  geom_ribbon(aes(date, ymin = 0, ymax = Diff), fill = "steelblue", alpha = 0.6) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0) +
  labs(title = "SafeCore Drawdown Relative to the Capped SWIX",
       subtitle = "Above zero: SafeCore fell less than its benchmark",
       x = "Year", y = "Difference in drawdown") +
  fmxdat::theme_fmx()

fmxdat::finplot(g_dd, y.pct = T, y.pct_acc = 1)
```

Over the full period, SafeCore has lower downside risk than the Capped SWIX on every measure. However, the drawdown plot shows that SafeCore’s advantage was mainly between 2015 and 2017 and in 2020. Since 2021, the difference has been close to zero or negative. Hence, its protection in down markets has weakened in recent years.

Next, we were asked to investigate where SafeCore's volatility comes from. A stock's weight does not tell you how much risk it adds, because that also depends on how volatile it is and how it moves with the rest of the fund. So I calculated each stock's contribution to the portfolio standard deviation over the last 12 months, using the average weights over that year. I then grouped this by sector and compared each sector's share of the weight with its share of the risk. Two stocks (PAN and VAL) had no sector in the SafeCore data, so I checked the index constituent data and classified both as Resources.

```{r Q1_B_Risk}
Risk_Contrib <- Q1_Risk_Contrib(Holdings = SafeCore, Stocks = Stocks, Months = 12)

Sectors <-
  SafeCore %>%
  group_by(Tickers) %>%
  filter(date == max(date)) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  select(Tickers, Sector)

Risk_Sector <-
  Risk_Contrib %>%
  left_join(Sectors, by = "Tickers") %>%
  # PAN and VAL have no sector in the SafeCore data but Index_Constituents lists both as Resources
  mutate(Sector = ifelse(Tickers %in% c("PAN", "VAL"), "Resources", Sector)) %>%
  group_by(Sector) %>%
  summarise(Weight = sum(wt), Risk = sum(Risk_Contrib)) %>%
  gather(Measure, Share, Weight, Risk)

g_risk <-
  Risk_Sector %>%
  ggplot() +
  geom_bar(aes(Sector, Share, fill = Measure), stat = "identity", position = "dodge") +
  labs(title = "Where SafeCore's Volatility Comes From",
       subtitle = "Share of portfolio weight and share of volatility by sector",
       x = "", y = "Share") +
  fmxdat::theme_fmx() + fmxdat::fmx_fills()

fmxdat::finplot(g_risk, y.pct = T, y.pct_acc = 1)
```

Resources make up just over a third of the fund but are responsible for around two thirds of its volatility, while financials and industrials add less volatility than their weight. Resource stocks depend on global commodity prices, which makes them exposed to offshore shocks.

For the factor exposures, the question asks for my own momentum and low volatility scores. For momentum I used the six month return excluding the most recent month, so that the score reflects a more persistent trend rather than the latest short-term move. For low volatility I used six months of daily realised volatility, reusing my rolling volatility function from Part A with a 126 day window. I flipped the sign so that less volatile stocks get a higher score and standardised both scores each month with `scale()` so they are on the same scale as the third-party scores. I then checked how closely my scores line up with the third-party ones each month.

```{r Q1_B_Scores}
Own_LowVol <-
  Stocks %>%
  Rolling_Vol(Window = 126) %>%
  mutate(YM = format(date, "%Y%B")) %>%
  group_by(Tickers, YM) %>%
  filter(date == last(date)) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  select(YM, Tickers, LowVol = RollSD)

Stock_Monthly <-
  Stocks %>%
  arrange(date) %>%
  group_by(Tickers) %>%
  mutate(Index = cumprod(1 + coalesce(Returns, 0))) %>%
  mutate(YM = format(date, "%Y%B")) %>%
  group_by(Tickers, YM) %>%
  filter(date == last(date)) %>%
  group_by(Tickers) %>%
  mutate(Ret = Index / lag(Index) - 1) %>%
  ungroup()

Own_Mom <-
  Stock_Monthly %>%
  group_by(Tickers) %>%
  mutate(Mom = lag(RcppRoll::roll_prod(1 + Ret, n = 6, fill = NA, align = "right")) - 1) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  select(YM, Tickers, Mom)

Scores <-
  inner_join(Own_Mom, Own_LowVol, by = c("YM", "Tickers")) %>%
  filter(!is.na(Mom), !is.na(LowVol)) %>%
  group_by(YM) %>%
  mutate(Own_Momentum = as.numeric(scale(Mom)),
         Own_LowVol = as.numeric(scale(-LowVol))) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  inner_join(Factor_Scores %>% mutate(YM = format(date, "%Y%B")) %>% spread(Factor, Factor_Value),
             by = c("YM", "Tickers"))

# Correlation across stocks each month between own and third-party scores
# Volatility Sensitivity is reversed so that a higher value means a less volatile stock
Score_Cor <-
  Scores %>%
  group_by(YM) %>%
  summarise(date = max(date),
            Momentum = cor(Own_Momentum, Momentum, use = "complete.obs"),
            `Low Volatility` = cor(Own_LowVol, -`Volatility Sensitivity`, use = "complete.obs")) %>%
  select(-YM) %>%
  gather(Factor, Correlation, -date)

g_cor <-
  Score_Cor %>%
  ggplot() +
  geom_line(aes(date, Correlation, color = Factor)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0) +
  labs(title = "Own vs Third-Party Factor Scores",
       subtitle = "Monthly correlation across stocks", x = "Year", y = "Correlation") +
  fmxdat::theme_fmx()

fmxdat::finplot(g_cor)
```

The own momentum score is closely related to the third-party momentum score in most months, apart from a short period in early 2021. The relationship between the own low volatility score and the third-party volatility sensitivity score is weaker. Since late 2022 the correlation has been positive in most months, which means the two scores mostly agree on which stocks are more volatile. However, the correlation is low and is negative in some periods, thus the two scores do not measure exactly the same thing.

The question asks for composite scores for different strategies to contextualise SafeCore’s scores. I therefore turned the stock scores into a portfolio score by taking the weighted average score of each portfolio’s holdings in the latest month, for SafeCore, the Capped SWIX and the strategy indices in the constituent data.

```{r Q1_B_Composite}
Last_Date <- max(SafeCore$date)

Weights <-
  bind_rows(
    SafeCore %>%
      filter(date == Last_Date) %>%
      select(Tickers, weight = Weight) %>%
      mutate(Portfolio = "SafeCore"),
    Cons %>%
      filter(date == Last_Date, Index %in% c("Capped SWIX", "LowVol", "Momentum", "Value", "Quality")) %>%
      select(Tickers, weight, Portfolio = Index)
  )

Composite <-
  Weights %>%
  left_join(Scores %>% filter(date == Last_Date), by = "Tickers") %>%
  group_by(Portfolio) %>%
  summarise(`Momentum (own)` = sum(weight * Own_Momentum, na.rm = T),
            `Low volatility (own)` = sum(weight * Own_LowVol, na.rm = T),
            Momentum = sum(weight * Momentum, na.rm = T),
            `Volatility Sensitivity` = sum(weight * `Volatility Sensitivity`, na.rm = T),
            Value = sum(weight * Value, na.rm = T),
            Growth = sum(weight * Growth, na.rm = T),
            `Earnings Quality` = sum(weight * `Earnings Quality`, na.rm = T)) %>%
  gather(Factor, Score, -Portfolio)

g_comp <-
  Composite %>%
  ggplot() +
  geom_bar(aes(Portfolio, Score, fill = Portfolio), stat = "identity") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0) +
  facet_wrap(~Factor, nrow = 2) +
  labs(title = "Composite Factor Scores",
       subtitle = "Weighted average score of each portfolio's holdings", x = "", y = "Score") +
  fmxdat::theme_fmx() + fmxdat::fmx_fills()

fmxdat::finplot(g_comp, x.vert = T)
```

SafeCore has a strong momentum tilt, and leans slightly towards value and earnings quality. Its own low volatility score is slightly below that of its benchmark, which suggests that it has no low volatility tilt.

## Part C

Here the question asks about the alpha opportunity since 2020 and how it changes with global macro factors. I used three pieces: dispersion, the average correlation between stocks, and a split by global uncertainty.

Dispersion measures how far constituent returns spread around the index return. High dispersion means more room for active managers to differentiate their portfolios. I used the dispersion function with a rolling 60 day (three month) window. I chose the weighted measure as my main one because SafeCore is managed against the Capped SWIX, so the opportunity that matters is the one relative to the index as it is actually weighted. I kept the unweighted measure on the plot for comparison. The constituent data starts in August 2020, so this covers the full period available since 2020.

```{r Q1_C_Disp, cache = TRUE}
J433_Cons <- Cons %>% filter(Index == "Capped SWIX")

BM <- Idx_Daily %>% filter(Tickers == "J433") %>% select(date, BM = Returns)

m3_disp <- Dispersion_Prep(df_used = J433_Cons, BMUse = BM, BMSel = "weight", NSel = 60) %>%
  filter(date >= ymd(20200101))

g_disp <-
  m3_disp %>%
  gather(Type, Value, starts_with("Dispersion")) %>%
  mutate(Type = ifelse(Type == "Dispersion_W", "Weighted", "Unweighted")) %>%
  ggplot() +
  geom_line(aes(date, Value, color = Type)) +
  labs(title = "Cross-Sectional Volatility (Dispersion)",
       subtitle = "Capped SWIX constituents (rolling 3 months)", x = "Year", y = "Dispersion") +
  fmxdat::theme_fmx() + fmxdat::fmx_cols()

fmxdat::finplot(g_disp, y.pct = T)
```

Dispersion is not constant, but increases rapidly in certain periods before returning to lower levels. These periods represent the times when the opportunity to differentiate a portfolio from the Capped SWIX was greatest.

Dispersion tells you how far apart returns are, but not whether stocks move in the same direction, so I also looked at correlations. For each month I built the correlation matrix of the constituents' daily returns and took the average across all pairs of stocks (leaving out the diagonal, since a stock is always perfectly correlated with itself). I wrote the function for one month and mapped it over all months.

```{r Q1_C_Cor}
Avg_Cor <- J433_Cons %>% fmxdat::YM() %>% group_split(YM) %>% map_df(~Q1_Month_Cor(.)) %>%
  filter(date >= ymd(20200101))

g_avgcor <-
  Avg_Cor %>%
  ggplot() +
  geom_line(aes(date, Avg_Cor), colour = "steelblue", linewidth = 0.8) +
  labs(title = "Average Correlation Between Constituents",
       subtitle = "Capped SWIX constituents (monthly)", x = "Year", y = "Average correlation") +
  fmxdat::theme_fmx()

fmxdat::finplot(g_avgcor)
```

The average correlation is generally low, but increases in certain periods, most notably in 2025 and 2026. Asset market correlations typically increase in periods of turmoil, as turmoil leads to asset market price homogeneity. A rolling correlation also keeps the noise, and a DCC estimate would give a cleaner, noise-reduced version of the comovement between stocks.

Finally, to link the alpha opportunity to a global macro factor, I used the global economic policy uncertainty index, since the seminar in the question focused on global policy uncertainty. I split the months into high uncertainty (above the 85th percentile), low uncertainty (below the 25th percentile) and other, and compared average dispersion and correlation in each group. I joined everything by year-month rather than by date, because month-end dates can differ between datasets.

```{r Q1_C_Enviro}
EPU <- Uncertainty %>% filter(Ticker == "EPUCGLCP Index") %>%
  fmxdat::YM() %>% group_by(YM) %>% filter(date == max(date)) %>% ungroup() %>%
  select(YM, EPU = TRI)

df_comp_plot <-
  left_join(
    m3_disp %>% fmxdat::YM() %>% group_by(YM) %>% filter(date == max(date)) %>% ungroup() %>% select(YM, Disp = Dispersion_W),
    Avg_Cor %>% fmxdat::YM() %>% select(YM, Cor = Avg_Cor),
    by = "YM"
  ) %>%
  left_join(EPU, by = "YM")

Enviro_Tab <-
  df_comp_plot %>% filter(!is.na(EPU), !is.na(Disp)) %>%
  rename(Value = EPU) %>%
  Enviro_Split(Hi = 0.85, Lo = 0.25, Label = "uncertainty") %>%
  group_by(Enviro) %>% summarise(Dispersion = mean(Disp), Correlation = mean(Cor, na.rm = T)) %>%
  rename(Environment = Enviro)

Enviro_Tab
```

Both dispersion and correlation are higher in high uncertainty months than in low uncertainty months. The higher correlation is consistent with turmoil leading to asset market price homogeneity. However, since high dispersion means that the alpha opportunity (the ability to differentiate portfolios) is high, this suggests that the alpha opportunity in the local market has increased with global policy uncertainty.

The seminar in the question was also about oil price volatility, so I repeated the same split using monthly oil price volatility (Brent crude) instead of policy uncertainty. I used the same cut-offs (85th and 25th percentiles) and the same `Enviro_Split` function, so the two can be compared directly.

```{r Q1_C_Oil}
Commods <- read_rds("Questions/Question1/data/Commodities.rds")

# Monthly oil price volatility (SD of daily returns within each month, annualised)
Oil_Vol <-
  Commods %>%
  filter(Ticker == "CO1 Comdty") %>%
  Q1_Level_to_Returns() %>%
  fmxdat::YM() %>% group_by(YM) %>%
  summarise(Oil_Vol = sd(Returns) * sqrt(252))

# Dispersion and correlation in high and low oil volatility months
Oil_Tab <-
  df_comp_plot %>%
  left_join(Oil_Vol, by = "YM") %>%
  filter(!is.na(Oil_Vol), !is.na(Disp)) %>%
  rename(Value = Oil_Vol) %>%
  Enviro_Split(Hi = 0.85, Lo = 0.25, Label = "oil volatility") %>%
  group_by(Enviro) %>% summarise(Dispersion = mean(Disp), Correlation = mean(Cor, na.rm = T)) %>%
  rename(Environment = Enviro)
```

To compare the two macro factors I put both splits in one graph.

```{r Q1_C_Enviro_Plot}
g_env <-
  bind_rows(Enviro_Tab %>% mutate(Factor = "Global policy uncertainty"),
            Oil_Tab %>% mutate(Factor = "Oil price volatility")) %>%
  # Keep only High, Low and Other as labels
  mutate(Environment = gsub(" uncertainty| oil volatility", "", Environment)) %>%
  mutate(Environment = factor(Environment, levels = c("Low", "Other", "High"))) %>%
  gather(Measure, Value, Dispersion, Correlation) %>%
  ggplot() +
  geom_point(aes(Environment, Value, color = Measure), size = 3) +
  geom_line(aes(Environment, Value, color = Measure, group = Measure)) +
  facet_wrap(~Factor) +
  labs(title = "Alpha Opportunity and Global Macro Conditions",
       subtitle = "Average dispersion and correlation in low, other and high months",
       caption = "Dispersion is the weighted spread of returns around the index. Correlation is the average pairwise correlation.",
       x = "", y = "") +
  fmxdat::theme_fmx() + fmxdat::fmx_cols()

fmxdat::finplot(g_env)
```

The pattern is the same for both macro factors. Dispersion and correlation both increase from low to high months, and the increase in correlation is largest when oil price volatility is high. The higher correlation is consistent with turmoil leading to asset market price homogeneity. However, since high dispersion means that the alpha opportunity (the ability to differentiate portfolios) is high, the alpha opportunity in the local market has increased with both global policy uncertainty and oil price volatility.

# Conclusion

Overall, local volatility is not much higher than it was before 2020. Instead, it is high in certain periods, mostly when offshore shocks occur. In 2026, the increase in volatility was largest in emerging markets.

SafeCore has outperformed its benchmark, but its protection in down markets has weakened in recent years. A large part of its volatility comes from resource stocks, and it leans towards stocks that have performed well recently rather than less volatile stocks. Therefore, it has limited protection against offshore shocks.

When global policy uncertainty is high, dispersion between stocks is higher, which means there is more opportunity for active managers to outperform the index.

Overall, I believe SafeCore would benefit from more protection against volatility, while still making use of the opportunities that arise during periods of high uncertainty.


# Question 2: Mid, Small and Large Cap Indices

Note: I did this question last so that is why so many functions from other questions become shared functions 

*Write-up* (Report) can be found at `Questions/Question2/Question2.pdf` (more detailed interpretations/explanations)

I initially kpet the html texevier folder for Question 2 and then only later realised the question requires a pdf output, so I recreated the folder with the PDF template to match Q1 and Q4.

```{r}
# Functions for this question:
list.files('Questions/Question2/code/', full.names = T, recursive = T) %>% .[grepl('.R', .)] %>% as.list() %>% walk(~source(.))
```

## Data

The weights in the constituent file don't always add up to one, so I rescaled them in each index and month first. I only kept the four index return series I needed. I gave a few objects a `Q2_` name here so they don't overwrite the Q1 objects with the same names.

```{r Q2_data}
Size_Idx <- read_rds("Questions/Question2/data/Monthly_Index_Constituents.rds")

Size_Clean <-
  Size_Idx %>%
  group_by(Fund, date) %>%
  mutate(Weight = Weight / sum(Weight)) %>%
  ungroup()

Q2_Idx_Daily <-
  read_rds("Questions/Question2/data/Index_Returns_Daily.rds") %>%
  filter(Tickers %in% c("J200", "J201", "J202", "J433"))

Q2_Stocks <- read_rds("Questions/Question2/data/Stock_Returns_Daily.rds")
```

## Sector exposure and concentration

The question asks about each index's sector exposure, so I plotted the weights per sector for each index over time. I used a stacked bar so it is easy to see how the split between sectors changes.

```{r Q2_sector}
g_sector <-
  Size_Clean %>%
  ggplot() +
  geom_bar(aes(date, Weight, fill = Sector), stat = "identity", width = 31) +
  facet_wrap(~Fund) +
  labs(title = "Sector Exposure by Index", subtitle = "Monthly constituent weights grouped by sector",
       x = "Year", y = "Sector weight") +
  fmxdat::theme_fmx() + fmxdat::fmx_fills()

fmxdat::finplot(g_sector, y.pct = T, y.pct_acc = 1)
```

Each index has quite a different sector mix. The large cap index was very heavy in resources at the start, the mid cap index used to be mostly industrials, and the small cap index has by far the most property. From the graph it is evident that each index poses a different sector risk.

For stock concentration I used the combined weight of the ten largest stocks in each index. I chose ten because the large cap index only has about 40 stocks.Because of this, a larger number (like 40) would show almost 100% the whole time and you wouldn't see any differences.

```{r Q2_conc}
Conc <-
  Size_Clean %>%
  group_by(Fund, date) %>%
  arrange(desc(Weight)) %>%
  top_n(10, Weight) %>%
  summarise(Top10 = sum(Weight))

g_conc <-
  Conc %>%
  ggplot() +
  geom_line(aes(date, Top10, color = Fund), alpha = 0.8) +
  labs(title = "Top 10 Stock Concentration", subtitle = "Combined weight of the ten largest stocks in each index",
       x = "Year", y = "Weight of top 10 stocks") +
  fmxdat::theme_fmx() + fmxdat::fmx_cols()

fmxdat::finplot(g_conc, y.pct = T, y.pct_acc = 1)
```

The large cap index is the most concentrated over the period, although this decreased after 2023. It remains the most concentrated by the end of the period, it is just slightly above the mid cap index at the end of the period. The mid cap index has become a lot more concentrated since 2020. The small cap index is the least concentrated over the whole period. Until around 2020, the Capped SWIX lies between the large cap index and the smaller indices. Therefore, an investor in the large cap index is more exposed to the performance of a few stocks than an investor in the small cap index.

## Volatility

The question asks about the volatility of the constituents, so I worked out a rolling one year SD for each stock and took the weighted average for each index at each month end. I moved my rolling vol function from Q1 into the root `code/` folder (`Rolling_Vol`), since Q1 and Q2 both use it. 

```{r Q2_consvol}
Cons_Vol <- Q2_Cons_Vol(Q2_Stocks, Size_Clean, Window = 252)

g_consvol <-
  Cons_Vol %>%
  ggplot() +
  geom_line(aes(date, RollSD, color = Fund), alpha = 0.8) +
  labs(title = "Realised Volatility of Index Constituents",
       subtitle = "Rolling 1 year standard deviation, annualised (weighted by index weight)",
       x = "Year", y = "Annualised SD") +
  fmxdat::theme_fmx() + fmxdat::fmx_cols()

fmxdat::finplot(g_consvol, y.pct = T, y.pct_acc = 1)
```

The volatility of all four indices increased in 2020 and stayed high for a year (as the 2020 returns remain in the one year window)). The small cap constituents are the most volatile for most of 2016 to 2022. The large cap index and the Capped SWIX follow almost the same path. From 2022 to 2024 the mid cap constituents are the least volatile. From 2025 the small cap constituents are the least volatile.

In class it was mentioned that in SA large cap stocks often look about as volatile as small caps (during the research paper topic discussions). Using a chart of the median peak-to-trough fall of stocks within a year, I wanted to see if the data shows the same.

```{r Q2_yeardd}
Stock_DD <-
  Q2_Stocks %>%
  filter(!is.na(Returns)) %>%
  arrange(date) %>%
  mutate(Year = format(date, "%Y")) %>%
  group_by(Tickers, Year) %>%
  mutate(CP = cumprod(1 + Returns)) %>%
  mutate(Drawdown = CP / cummax(CP) - 1) %>%
  summarise(Max_DD = min(Drawdown))

Year_DD <-
  Size_Clean %>%
  filter(format(date, "%m") == "12", date >= ymd(20151201)) %>%
  mutate(Year = format(date, "%Y")) %>%
  left_join(Stock_DD, by = c("Tickers", "Year")) %>%
  group_by(Fund, Year) %>%
  summarise(Median_DD = median(Max_DD, na.rm = T))

g_dd <-
  Year_DD %>%
  ggplot() +
  geom_bar(aes(Year, Median_DD, fill = Fund), stat = "identity", position = "dodge") +
  labs(title = "Peak-to-Trough Falls of Index Constituents",
       subtitle = "Median of each stock's largest fall from its peak within the year",
       x = "Year", y = "Largest fall from peak") +
  fmxdat::theme_fmx() + fmxdat::fmx_fills()

fmxdat::finplot(g_dd, y.pct = T, y.pct_acc = 1, x.vert = T)
```

It does! The typical stock falls by about the same amount in every size index, with 2020 being the worst year for all of them. This suggests that the large cap index is about as risky as the small cap index.

For the stratification I split the months into high volatility, low volatility and other, based on the Capped SWIX's own monthly volatility. I used the same cut-offs as in Q1 and Q3 (85th and 25th percentiles) so the questions are consistent. This time I put the split into a function in the root `code/` folder (`Enviro_Split`) so it can be reused.

```{r Q2_strat}
Idxs <-
  Q2_Idx_Daily %>%
  mutate(Fund = ifelse(Tickers == "J200", "LargeCaps",
                ifelse(Tickers == "J201", "MidCaps",
                ifelse(Tickers == "J202", "SmallCaps", "CappedSWIX")))) %>%
  select(date, Tickers = Fund, Return = Returns) %>%
  filter(!is.na(Return)) %>%
  mutate(YM = format(date, "%Y%B"))

SWIX_Vol <-
  Idxs %>%
  filter(Tickers == "CappedSWIX") %>%
  group_by(YM) %>% summarise(Value = sd(Return) * sqrt(252)) %>%
  Enviro_Split(Hi = 0.85, Lo = 0.25, Label = "volatility") %>%
  select(YM, Enviro)

left_join(Idxs, SWIX_Vol, by = "YM") %>%
  group_by(Enviro, Tickers) %>%
  summarise(SD = sd(Return) * sqrt(252), Ret = mean(Return) * 252) %>%
  ungroup()
```

All four indices have a negative average return in high volatility months, and the small cap index falls the most. However, the small cap index has the lowest standard deviation in every group. This is despite its constituents being about as volatile as those of the large cap index.

The small cap index had the lowest SD in every group, even though its stocks are just as volatile as the large cap stocks. I wanted to find out why. I first thought about fitting a GARCH model to each index (the question said we may use volatility models), but that would mostly repeat the stats table and what I did in Q1. I hadn't used PCA anywhere yet, so I tried that instead. I used log returns. The rest of Q2 uses simple returns because those get chained into monthly and rolling returns. The idea was to check whether small cap stocks move together less, which would explain the lower index volatility. 

```{r Q2_pca}
PCA <-
  Size_Clean %>%
  filter(format(date, "%m") == "12", date >= ymd(20151201)) %>%
  group_split(Fund, date) %>%
  map_df(~Q2_PCA(., Q2_Stocks))

g_pca <-
  PCA %>%
  ggplot() +
  geom_bar(aes(Year, Prop, fill = Fund), stat = "identity", position = "dodge") +
  labs(title = "Eigenvalue Proportions of Index Constituents",
       subtitle = "Proportion of variation explained by the first principal component, per calendar year",
       x = "Year", y = "Proportion of variation (PC 1)") +
  fmxdat::theme_fmx() + fmxdat::fmx_fills()

fmxdat::finplot(g_pca, y.pct = T, y.pct_acc = 1, x.vert = T)
```

They do! The large cap index has the highest proportion in every year and the small cap index has the lowest. This suggests that small cap stocks are affected more by idiosyncratic information. Although the small cap constituents are volatile, they move together less. Therefore, their movements partly offset each other, and the small cap index has the lowest volatility.

## Returns

For returns I used rolling 3 year returns instead of cumulative returns, because a good or bad start can skew a cumulative return plot for the whole period. I also put the daily to monthly conversion I used in Q1 and Q3 into a shared function (`Daily_to_Monthly`).

```{r Q2_rollrets}
Idx_Monthly <-
  Q2_Idx_Daily %>%
  Daily_to_Monthly() %>%
  mutate(Fund = ifelse(Tickers == "J200", "LargeCaps",
                ifelse(Tickers == "J201", "MidCaps",
                ifelse(Tickers == "J202", "SmallCaps", "CappedSWIX"))))

g_roll <-
  Idx_Monthly %>%
  group_by(Fund) %>%
  mutate(RollRets = RcppRoll::roll_prod(1 + Ret, 36, fill = NA, align = "right") ^ (12/36) - 1) %>%
  group_by(date) %>% filter(any(!is.na(RollRets))) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  ggplot() +
  geom_line(aes(date, RollRets, color = Fund), alpha = 0.8) +
  labs(title = "Rolling 3 Year Annualised Returns", subtitle = "Size indices compared to the Capped SWIX",
       x = "Year", y = "Rolling 3 year return (Ann.)") +
  fmxdat::theme_fmx() + fmxdat::fmx_cols()

fmxdat::finplot(g_roll, y.pct = T, y.pct_acc = 1)
```

The small cap index has the widest range of rolling returns. It had the lowest rolling returns around 2020 and the highest from 2022 to 2024. By the end of the sample, all four indices have similar rolling returns.

I then used the same stats table as in Q1 (Capped SWIX as the benchmark) to compare the risk and return profiles over the last 3 and 5 years.

```{r Q2_stats}
Q2_Tab_stats <-
  bind_rows(
    Moments_Comp(Idx_Monthly %>% select(date, Tickers, Ret), BM = "J433", Yrs_LookBack = 3, NA_Check = 0.8),
    Moments_Comp(Idx_Monthly %>% select(date, Tickers, Ret), BM = "J433", Yrs_LookBack = 5, NA_Check = 0.8)
  )

Q2_Tab_stats
```

The small cap index has the highest annualised return and the lowest standard deviation over both periods, and therefore the highest adjusted Sharpe ratio. The large cap index behaved most like the benchmark, although with slightly more market risk. The mid cap index has the lowest return over both periods.

## Active share

Active share wasn't in the course material, so I used the standard formula (half the sum of the absolute differences between the index weights and the Capped SWIX weights). A stock that is only in one of the two gets a weight of 0 in the other.

```{r Q2_as}
Active_Share <-
  Size_Clean %>%
  select(date, Tickers, Fund, Weight) %>%
  spread(Fund, Weight, fill = 0) %>%
  gather(Fund, Weight, LargeCaps, MidCaps, SmallCaps) %>%
  group_by(date, Fund) %>%
  summarise(AS = 0.5 * sum(abs(Weight - CappedSWIX))) %>%
  ungroup()

g_as <-
  Active_Share %>%
  ggplot() +
  geom_line(aes(date, AS, color = Fund), alpha = 0.8) +
  labs(title = "Active Share Relative to the Capped SWIX",
       subtitle = "Half the sum of absolute weight differences from the Capped SWIX",
       x = "Year", y = "Active share") +
  fmxdat::theme_fmx() + fmxdat::fmx_cols()

fmxdat::finplot(g_as, y.pct = T, y.pct_acc = 1)
```

The large cap index has the lowest active share, which means it holds largely the same stocks as the Capped SWIX at similar weights. The small cap index has an active share close to one throughout. Therefore, the small cap index gives an investor the most different set of stocks from the benchmark.

## Summary

Each index carries a different sector exposure. The large cap index is the most concentrated, its stocks show the most comovement and it is the most similar to the Capped SWIX, with a beta above one. The mid cap index has had the lowest returns in recent years. Within each year, the typical small cap stock falls about as much from its peak as the typical large cap stock. However, small cap stocks move together the least. Therefore, the small cap index has the lowest volatility and the highest risk-adjusted return over the last three and five years. It is also the most different from the benchmark, but it had the largest losses in high volatility months. Overall, the results do not support the view that small caps are the most volatile part of the local market.

# Question 3: Portfolio Return Comparison

The slides can be found in `Questions/Question3/` (knitted with `powerpoint_presentation`).

For this question I made PowerPoint slides comparing ABC Fund to its peers, using returns only. The slides are in `Questions/Question3/`. I worked through the manager's suggested points in order.

```{r Q3_Source}
# Question 3 functions
list.files('Questions/Question3/code/', full.names = T, recursive = T) %>% .[grepl('.R', .)] %>% as.list() %>% walk(~source(.))
```

```{r Q3_Data}
Active_Manager_Peers <- read_rds("Questions/Question3/data/Active_Managers.rds")
ABC_Fund <- read_rds("Questions/Question3/data/ABC_Fund.rds")
Idx_Daily <- read_rds("Questions/Question3/data/Index_Returns_Daily.rds")
Monthly_Cons <- read_rds("Questions/Question3/data/Monthly_Index_Constituents.rds")
Stocks <- read_rds("Questions/Question3/data/Stock_Returns_Daily.rds")
```

The fund returns are monthly and the index returns are daily, so I converted the indices to monthly returns (same as for SafeCore in Q1). I joined on a year-month label because the month-end dates differ between funds and indices.

```{r Q3_Monthly}
# Monthly returns for the Capped SWIX and the style indices
# Chain daily returns into an index, keep the last trading day of each month and take month-on-month returns
Idx_Monthly <-
  Idx_Daily %>%
  arrange(date) %>%
  group_by(Tickers) %>%
  mutate(Index = cumprod(1 + Returns)) %>%
  mutate(YM = format(date, "%Y%B")) %>%
  group_by(Tickers, YM) %>%
  filter(date == last(date)) %>%
  group_by(Tickers) %>%
  mutate(Ret = Index / lag(Index) - 1) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  filter(!is.na(Ret)) %>%
  select(YM, Tickers, Ret)

# Benchmark (Capped SWIX) monthly returns
BM_Monthly <- Idx_Monthly %>% filter(Tickers == "J433") %>% select(YM, BM_Monthly = Ret)

# Peers and ABC Fund in one data frame, with the same month label for joining
Funds <-
  bind_rows(Active_Manager_Peers, ABC_Fund) %>%
  arrange(date) %>%
  mutate(YM = format(date, "%Y%B"))
```

## Point 1: Rolling 3 year beta

I used the rolling beta function from the mapping prac, changing only the column name and joining on `YM`. The benchmark only starts in 2015, so I dropped earlier fund months.

```{r Q3_Roll_Beta, cache = TRUE}
# Rolling 36 month regression of each fund on the Capped SWIX (months with benchmark data only)
Manager_list <- Funds %>% filter(YM %in% BM_Monthly$YM) %>% group_split(Name)

Rolling_Beta <-
  Manager_list %>%
  map_df(~Q3_Roll_Regression(., BM_Monthly, Nsel = 36, Silent = TRUE)) %>%
  arrange(date)
```

The plot is a boxplot and jitter (with ABC added as a red dot). I averaged over 5 years instead of 10 ( the betas only start in 2018). I also used plain labels so the manager can read it.

```{r Q3_Beta_Plot}
Q3_Beta_Boxplot(Rolling_Beta, Months_back = 60, Fund = "ABC_Fund")
```

Most active managers sit close to the market line, so their returns mostly follow the market. ABC sits below almost all of its peers.

## Point 2: What drives ABC Fund's returns

I wanted to use the TidyFit package for this, but it didn't work out as I had hoped. I then pivoted to regressing returns on the Capped SWIX (market) and the style indices. I compared ABC to the average peer to keep the slide simple.

```{r Q3_Factor_Data}
# Market and style index returns in columns (Low Vol left out as it only starts in 2024)
Factors <-
  Idx_Monthly %>%
  filter(Tickers %in% c("J433", "STXVALJ433", "STXMOMJ433", "J202")) %>%
  spread(Tickers, Ret) %>%
  select(YM, Market = J433, Value = STXVALJ433, Momentum = STXMOMJ433, Small_Caps = J202)

# ABC Fund returns joined to the factor returns
ABC_df <- Funds %>%
  filter(Name == "ABC_Fund") %>%
  select(YM, Returns) %>%
  left_join(Factors, by = "YM") %>%
  drop_na()

# Average peer return each month joined to the factor returns
Peer_df <- Funds %>%
  filter(Name != "ABC_Fund") %>%
  group_by(YM) %>%
  # Average return across all peers in each month (peers without a return that month are skipped)
  summarise(Returns = mean(Returns, na.rm = T)) %>%
  left_join(Factors, by = "YM") %>%
  drop_na()
```

`tidyfit::regress` gave a package error, so I used `lm` directly (which is what `m("lm")` runs).

```{r Q3_Factor_Reg}
# lm used directly as tidyfit::regress returned an error (slice_id not found)
lm_ABC  <- lm(Returns ~ Market + Value + Momentum + Small_Caps, data = ABC_df)
lm_Peer <- lm(Returns ~ Market + Value + Momentum + Small_Caps, data = Peer_df)

# Exposures of both in one table
Loadings <-
  bind_rows(lm_ABC %>% broom::tidy() %>% mutate(Name = "ABC Fund"),
    lm_Peer %>% broom::tidy() %>% mutate(Name = "Average peer")) %>%
  # Intercept removed so that only the factor exposures are shown
  filter(term != "(Intercept)")
```

```{r Q3_Factor_Pvalues}
Loadings %>% select(Name, term, estimate, p.value)
```

```{r Q3_Factor_Plot}
g_fac <- Loadings %>%
  mutate(term = gsub("_", " ", term)) %>%
  ggplot() +
  geom_bar(aes(term, estimate, fill = Name), stat = "identity", position = "dodge") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0) +
  labs(title = "What drives the returns of ABC Fund compared to the average peer",
       subtitle = "Above zero: returns move with that part of the market. Below zero: returns move against it", x = "", y = "Exposure") +
  fmxdat::theme_fmx() + fmxdat::fmx_fills()

g_fac
```

The average peer is mainly driven by the market (large and highly significant market exposure). ABC is different as its only significant exposure is to momentum (at the 5% level). Thus, ts returns respond to stocks that have done well recently and does not follow the market. Thus, this suggests ABC’s returns are driven differently from its peers.

I made a mistake in Point 2. I didn't check properly and discovered later that the Low Vol index only starts in 2024. Including it reduced the regression down to only 21 months. Dropping it gives 7 years of data which is much more sensible !

## Point 3: Relative performance over time

For relative performance over time I used rolling 3 year returns, since cumulative returns are distorted by different start dates. To compare ABC to its peers, I calculated the share of peers that ABC beat each month. I coloured the periods where ABC beat more than half of its peers green, and red otherwise.

```{r Q3_Share_Data}
# Rolling 3 year annualised return of every fund
Roll_Funds <- Funds %>%
  arrange(date) %>%
  group_by(Name) %>%
  mutate(RollRet = RcppRoll::roll_prod(1+Returns, n = 36, fill = NA, align = "right")^(12/36) - 1) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  filter(!is.na(RollRet))

# ABC Fund's rolling return in its own column
ABC_Roll <- Roll_Funds %>% filter(Name == "ABC_Fund") %>% select(YM, ABC = RollRet)

# Share of peers with a lower rolling return than ABC Fund each month
df_comp <- Roll_Funds %>%
  filter(Name != "ABC_Fund") %>%
  left_join(ABC_Roll, by = "YM") %>%
  filter(!is.na(ABC)) %>%
  mutate(XS = ABC - RollRet) %>%
  group_by(date) %>%
  summarise(Proportion = sum(XS>0)/n())
```

```{r Q3_Share_Plot}
g_share <- df_comp %>%
  ggplot() +
  # Green when ABC Fund beat more than half of its peers, red when it beat fewer
  geom_ribbon(aes(date, ymin = 0.5, ymax = ifelse(Proportion > 0.5, Proportion, 0.5)), fill = "darkgreen", alpha = 0.4) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(date, ymin = ifelse(Proportion < 0.5, Proportion, 0.5), ymax = 0.5), fill = "darkred", alpha = 0.4) +
  geom_line(aes(date, Proportion), colour = "grey30", size = 1) +
  # Half of peers beaten
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0.5) +
  labs(title = "ABC Fund has outperformed most of its peers for most of the last decade",
       subtitle = "Share of peers with a lower rolling 3 year return than ABC Fund",
       caption = "Green: ABC Fund beat more than half of its peers. Red: ABC Fund beat fewer than half.",
       x = "Year", y = "Share of peers beaten") +
  fmxdat::theme_fmx()

fmxdat::finplot(g_share, x.date.dist = "1 year", x.date.type = "%Y", x.vert = T, y.pct = T, y.pct_acc = 1)
```

ABC beat most of its peers for most of the period, especially from 2020 to 2022 (which was a downturn period during and after the pandemic). It dipped in 2019 and again in 2025 (fell below half of its peers). The manager should be aware of this recent weakness before taking the stage because clients will likely ask about it!

## Point 4: Does ABC do well when dispersion is high?

The manager believes his fund does well when market dispersion is high. To test this, I calculated the rolling 12 month dispersion of the Capped SWIX constituents (as in Q1) and split the months into high dispersion (above the 85th percentile), low (below the 25th) and other. I then compared ABC's average 12 month return above the market with the average peer's in each group.

```{r Q3_Disp, cache = TRUE}
# Capped SWIX month-end weights
# Shifted forward one month so each month uses the weights known at its start
J433_W <-
  Monthly_Cons %>%
  filter(Fund == "CappedSWIX") %>%
  mutate(YM = format(date %m+% months(1), "%Y%B")) %>%
  select(YM, Tickers, weight = Weight)

# Daily stock returns with their Capped SWIX weights
J433_Cons <-
  Stocks %>%
  # Month label to match the weights
  mutate(YM = format(date, "%Y%B")) %>%
  # Keep only stocks in the Capped SWIX that month
  inner_join(J433_W, by = c("YM", "Tickers")) %>%
  # Drop stocks without a return that day
  filter(!is.na(Returns)) %>%
  # Rescale the weights to add up to one each day (the file does not cover the full index)
  group_by(date) %>%
  mutate(weight = weight / sum(weight)) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  # Column names used by the dispersion function
  select(date, Tickers, Return = Returns, weight)

# Benchmark (Capped SWIX) daily returns
BM <- Idx_Daily %>% filter(Tickers == "J433") %>% select(date, BM = Returns)

# Rolling 12 month (250 day) dispersion
ann_disp <- Dispersion_Prep(df_used = J433_Cons, BMUse = BM, BMSel = "weight", NSel = 250)
```

```{r Q3_Enviro}
# Month-end dispersion
Disp_M <-
  ann_disp %>%
  mutate(YM = format(date, "%Y%B")) %>%
  group_by(YM) %>% filter(date == last(date)) %>% ungroup() %>%
  select(YM, Value = Dispersion_W)

# Fund returns joined to dispersion, split into high, low and other, then averaged
Enviro_Tab <-
  Q3_Rel_12m(Funds, BM_Monthly, Fund = "ABC_Fund") %>%
  left_join(Disp_M, by = "YM") %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  filter(!is.na(Value)) %>%
  Enviro_Split(Hi = 0.85, Lo = 0.25, Label = "dispersion") %>%
  group_by(Enviro, Group) %>%
  summarise(XS = mean(XS))
```

```{r Q3_Dispersion}
g_disp <-
  Enviro_Tab %>%
  ggplot() +
  geom_bar(aes(Enviro, XS, fill = Group), stat = "identity", position = "dodge") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0) +
  labs(title = "ABC Fund compared to the average peer when market dispersion is high and low",
       subtitle = "Average 12 month return above the market (Capped SWIX)",
       caption = "High dispersion: stock returns differ a lot from the market, so there is more room for active managers to differ.",
       x = "", y = "Return above the market") +
  fmxdat::theme_fmx() + fmxdat::fmx_fills()

fmxdat::finplot(g_disp, y.pct = T, y.pct_acc = 0.1)
```

Over the longer period, the data supports the manager's claim. In high dispersion months ABC beat the market while the average peer fell below it, and this is where ABC's advantage over its peers was largest.

A note on a mistake I made: I first only used the constituent file from Q1 (which only starts in 2020) and assumed that was all the dispersion data available. Over that short period ABC did not do better in high dispersion. When I realised the monthly weights go back much further the next morning and redid it with the full history, I made the necessary changes and the result reversed! The short period was mostly the last few years, when ABC's performance was weaker (Point 3). This is still something I think the manager should keep in mind...


# Question 4: Portfolio Construction

*Write-up* (Report) can be found at `Questions/Question4/Question4.pdf`

```{r}
# Functions for this question:
list.files('Questions/Question4/code/', full.names = T, recursive = T) %>% .[grepl('.R', .)] %>% as.list() %>% walk(~source(.))
```

I googled what a balanced index fund is just to be sure. The first thing that came up was the Satrix Balanced Index Fund fact sheet (Can be found at this link: https://satrix.co.za/media/93236?inline=true). It holds a mix of the key local and international asset classes, and aims to grow capital and provide income while reducing volatility compared to an equity-only portfolio. This is the kind of fund the question asks for, except that the weights are updated every quarter.

## Data

I gave a few objects a `Q4_` name here so they don't overwrite the objects with the same names from the other questions.

```{r Q4_data}
Q4_MSCI <- read_rds("Questions/Question4/data/MSCI_Indexes.rds")
Bond_Yields <- read_rds("Questions/Question4/data/Global_Bond_Yields.rds")
Commods <- read_rds("Questions/Question4/data/Commodities.rds")
Q4_Idx_Daily <- read_rds("Questions/Question4/data/Index_Returns_Daily.rds")
LCL_Yield <- read_rds("Questions/Question4/data/Monthly_LCL_Yield_Indexes.rds")
STeFI <- read_rds("Questions/Question4/data/STeFI_Index.rds")
```

## Choosing the assets

I used the assets the question mentions as my starting point. For global equity I used the MSCI USA, Europe, Japan and EM indices instead of a world index. A world index already has these in it and would count the same stocks twice. The question asks for large and mid caps for local equity, and I used the J200 and J201 for these. For the two factor indices I used value and momentum, since low vol only starts in 2024 and would fail the 5 year rule anyway (I learnt this the hard way in Q3). I also added the ALBI, CILI and listed property (J253) because the question lists them. On top of those I added three 10 year government bonds, gold and the commodity index. I left out oil because it is already in the commodity index.

The global indices are in USD and the local ones in ZAR. I checked all the data files for a USD/ZAR rate to convert them but there wasn't one (SAVIUSD is only the volatility of the rand). This is something to keep in mind with the results.

## Bond returns

The paper gives the bond data as yields and I needed returns first. I remembered the standard formula from previous coursework, but I googled it as well and found a Quant Stack Exchange answer (https://quant.stackexchange.com/questions/22837/how-to-calculate-us-treasury-total-return-from-yield/57403#57403) that gives the monthly return as the interest (yield divided by 12) minus duration times the change in yield. I purposefully left out convexity because it matters less for small changes. It is a rough proxy (convexity left out and fixed modified duration) and I would treat the bond results with some caution.

To pick the duration, I checked the average 10 year yields since 2010.

```{r Q4_avg_yields}
Bond_Yields %>%
  filter(Name %in% c("US_10Yr", "Germany_10Yr", "UK_10Yr"), date >= as.Date("2010-01-01")) %>%
  group_by(Name) %>%
  summarise(Avg_Yield = mean(TRI))
```

The average across the three is about 2.1%. I then used the duration formula for a 10 year bond with half-yearly coupons equal to its yield. 

```{r Q4_duration}
# average yield of the three bonds (in decimals)
i <- 0.0211

# (20 half-year periods) coupon each period and the principal at the end
t <- 1:20
CashFlow <- c(rep(i / 2 * 100, 19), 100 + i / 2 * 100)

# cash flows discounted at the yield
PV_CashFlow <- CashFlow / (1 + i / 2)^t

# Macaulay duration, then modified duration
Mac_D <- sum(t * PV_CashFlow) / (2 * sum(PV_CashFlow))
Mac_D / (1 + i / 2)
```

This gives a modified duration of about 9. I used 9 for all three bonds.

## Monthly returns for all assets

I put each asset's class and region in a small table since the limits are set per group. Then I built one table of monthly returns. The local indices are daily returns. I chained them into an index first and took month-end returns (the same way as in Q3). The files also end their months on different days (trading day vs calendar day). I used one date per year-month so that all the assets line up.

```{r Q4_universe}
# Asset class and region of each asset (used for the group limits)
ref <- bind_rows(
  tibble(Name = c("MSCI_USA", "MSCI_EU", "MSCI_Jap", "MSCI_EM"),
         Class = "Equity", Region = "Global"),
  tibble(Name = c("J200", "J201", "STXVALJ433", "STXMOMJ433", "J253"),
         Class = "Equity", Region = "Local"),
  tibble(Name = c("US_10Yr", "Germany_10Yr", "UK_10Yr"),
         Class = "Bonds", Region = "Global"),
  tibble(Name = c("ALBITR", "CILITR"),
         Class = "Bonds", Region = "Local"),
  tibble(Name = c("Gold", "Bcom_Index"),
         Class = "Commodities", Region = "Global")
)

Q4_Returns <- Q4_Build_Fund(Q4_MSCI, Bond_Yields, Commods, Q4_Idx_Daily, LCL_Yield, ref)

# start date and months of data for each asset
Q4_Returns %>%
  group_by(Name) %>%
  summarise(Start = format(min(date), "%b %Y"), Months = n()) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  arrange(desc(Months))
```

The local equity indices start later than the rest (J200 and J201 in 2015, momentum in 2017 and value in 2018). With the 5 year rule they only come into the fund later on.

## Limits and gap filling

The limits in the question are per group (equity, bonds, commodities and global). Each group gets its limit in a small table and this is turned into `Amat` and `bvec` for `quadprog`. The upper limits are multiplied by minus one since `solve.QP` only works with "greater than or equal to" constraints.

The question says to use at least 10 years of data but only to drop assets with less than 5 years. This means momentum and value have gaps in the 10 year window. A covariance matrix can't have gaps. I filled them with the `impute_missing_returns` function, using random draws from each asset's own return distribution.

## Optimising every quarter

I went with minimum variance since it doesn’t need return forecasts and this is usually where optimisers struggle. I re-optimised the fund at every quarter-end. Each time it takes the last 10 years of monthly returns, keeps assets with at least 5 years of data, fills the gaps, estimates a Ledoit-Wolf covariance matrix and solves for the weights. The covariance uses data from 2010 and the first rebalance is at the end of 2019. 

```{r Q4_roll_weights, cache = TRUE}
# wide return matrix from 2010 onwards
return_mat <-
  Q4_Returns %>%
  filter(date >= ymd(20100101)) %>%
  select(date, Name, Returns) %>%
  spread(Name, Returns)

# quarter-end rebalance dates
EOM_datevec <-
  return_mat %>% select(date) %>% unique %>%
  mutate(YM = format(date, "%Y%B")) %>% group_by(YM) %>% filter(date == last(date)) %>% ungroup() %>%
  mutate(Months = as.numeric(format(date, format = "%m"))) %>% filter(Months %in% c(3, 6, 9, 12)) %>%
  pull(date) %>% unique

# minimum variance weights at each rebalance date
Q4_Weights <-
  EOM_datevec %>% map_df(~Q4_Roll_Optimizer(return_mat, EOM_datevec = ., ref, LookBackSel = 120))
```

I checked that the weights sum to 1 and stay within all the limits on every date (and that the solver never failed). The bond, commodity and global limits are binding every quarter. This means the split between asset classes stays fixed and the optimiser just picks the assets within each class.

## Comparing the fund

To compare the fund, I set up a fixed-weight portfolio using the strategic benchmark weights from the Satrix fact sheet. I used the closest indices I had (Capped SWIX, MSCI World, MSCI EM, ALBI, J253 and STeFI for cash) and added their small global infrastructure and global property weights to MSCI World. It is only an approximation and not the actual fund, so in the write-up I just call it a strategic balanced allocation. Its weights get reset on the same quarter-end dates as the fund. I also added the Capped SWIX on its own as an equity-only comparison. The portfolio returns use Safe_Return.portfolio, the same as for SafeCore in Q1.

```{r Q4_port_returns}
# minimum variance fund returns
MinVol_Rets <- Q4_Port_Returns(Weights = Q4_Weights %>% select(date, Tickers, Weight = minvol),
                               Returns = Q4_Returns %>% select(date, Tickers = Name, Returns),
                               Name = "Minimum variance")

# monthly returns for the strategic balanced allocation
ref_bm <- tibble(Name = c("J433", "MSCI_AllWorld", "MSCI_EM", "ALBITR", "J253", "STEFI"))
BM_Returns <- Q4_Build_Fund(Q4_MSCI, Bond_Yields, Commods,
                            bind_rows(Q4_Idx_Daily, STeFI %>% select(date, Tickers, Returns)),
                            LCL_Yield, ref_bm)

# fixed weights, reset on the same quarter-end dates as the fund
Port_BM <- tibble(Tickers = c("J433", "MSCI_AllWorld", "MSCI_EM", "ALBITR", "J253", "STEFI"),
                  Weight  = c(0.40, 0.30, 0.08, 0.17, 0.03, 0.02))

BM_Weights <- unique(Q4_Weights$date) %>% map_df(~Port_BM %>% mutate(date = .x))

Q4_BM_Rets <- Q4_Port_Returns(Weights = BM_Weights,
                              Returns = BM_Returns %>% select(date, Tickers = Name, Returns),
                              Name = "Strategic balanced allocation")

# equity-only comparison: Capped SWIX over the same months
SWIX_Rets <-
  BM_Returns %>%
  filter(Name == "J433", date > min(Q4_Weights$date)) %>%
  select(date, Returns) %>%
  mutate(Tickers = "Capped SWIX")

All_Rets <- bind_rows(MinVol_Rets, Q4_BM_Rets, SWIX_Rets)
```

## Results

All three start in January 2020. This means the cumulative returns aren't distorted by different start dates (unlike in Q3).

```{r Q4_cum}
g_cum <-
  All_Rets %>%
  arrange(date) %>%
  group_by(Tickers) %>%
  mutate(CP = cumprod(1 + Returns)) %>%
  mutate(CP = CP / first(CP)) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  ggplot() +
  geom_line(aes(date, CP, color = Tickers)) +
  labs(title = "Cumulative Returns",
       subtitle = "Minimum variance fund vs strategic balanced allocation and Capped SWIX",
       x = "", y = "Growth of R1 invested in 2020",
       caption = "Note:\nAll portfolios start in January 2020.") +
  fmxdat::theme_fmx(CustomCaption = T)

fmxdat::finplot(g_cum)
```

All three start in January 2020, so the comparison isn’t distorted by different start dates. The fund lost less than both comparisons in the 2020 decline. However, it grew more slowly from 2022 and ends below both the strategic balanced allocation and the Capped SWIX. This suggests the fund offers more protection when markets fall but gives up some of the gains when they rise.

Drawdown plots are good for a risk-sensitive client like a balanced fund, so I added one (same as in Q1).

```{r Q4_dd}
g_dd <-
  All_Rets %>%
  arrange(date) %>%
  group_by(Tickers) %>%
  mutate(CP = cumprod(1 + Returns)) %>%
  mutate(Drawdown = CP / cummax(CP) - 1) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  ggplot() +
  geom_line(aes(date, Drawdown, color = Tickers)) +
  labs(title = "Drawdowns: Minimum Variance Fund and Comparison Portfolios",
       subtitle = "Fall from the previous peak",
       x = "", y = "Drawdown") +
  fmxdat::theme_fmx()

fmxdat::finplot(g_dd, y.pct = T, y.pct_acc = 1)
```

The drawdowns show how far each portfolio falls from its previous peak. The fund had the smallest drawdown in 2020 and near the end of the sample. In 2022, however, its drawdown was similar to the strategic balanced allocation. Therefore, the lower volatility didn’t always lead to smaller losses.

I then used the same stats table as in Q1 and Q2, with the strategic balanced allocation as the benchmark.

```{r Q4_stats}
Q4_Tab_stats <-
  bind_rows(
    Moments_Comp(All_Rets %>% select(date, Tickers, Ret = Returns), BM = "Strategic balanced allocation", Yrs_LookBack = 3, NA_Check = 0.8),
    Moments_Comp(All_Rets %>% select(date, Tickers, Ret = Returns), BM = "Strategic balanced allocation", Yrs_LookBack = 5, NA_Check = 0.8)
  )

Q4_Tab_stats
```

The fund has the lowest volatility, the smallest average drawdown and the smallest modified CVaR over both periods. Its beta is below one, which means it moves less than the benchmark. However, it earned less than the benchmark over five years and its information ratio is negative over both periods. Over three years it got a similar return to the Capped SWIX with much lower volatility. This shows that the fund achieves lower risk, but at the cost of some return.

Lastly I plotted the weights at each rebalance as a stacked bar, with the assets ordered by class.

```{r Q4_weights_plot}
g_wts <-
  Q4_Weights %>%
  mutate(Tickers = factor(Tickers, levels = ref$Name)) %>%
  ggplot() +
  geom_bar(aes(date, minvol, fill = Tickers), stat = "identity") +
  labs(title = "Weights Plot",
       subtitle = "Stacked bar of the fund weights at each quarterly rebalance",
       x = "", y = "Weight") +
  fmxdat::theme_fmx()

fmxdat::finplot(g_wts, y.pct = T, y.pct_acc = 1)
```

The bond, commodity and global limits bind at every rebalance, so the split between asset classes stays the same over the whole sample period. The optimiser mainly decides which assets to hold within each class. For example, the fund held mostly US bonds until 2023 and then moved towards German bonds, while inflation-linked bonds were held throughout. Gold makes up most of the commodity weight. The local equity indexes only come in once they have five years of data, and MSCI Japan has the largest global equity weight. Part of this preference for global assets may be due to the USD/ZAR mix, so the weights should be interpreted with caution.

## Summary

Overall, the fund achieves lower risk than both comparisons. It had the lowest volatility and lost the least during the 2020 decline. However, it also earned lower returns, and its losses were not always smaller than the benchmark’s (2022). The limits on bonds, commodities and global assets were binding throughout, so the split between asset classes was mostly set by the limits and the optimiser mainly chose the assets within each class. With the short sample, the USD/ZAR mix and the bond proxy, I wouldn’t read too much into the exact numbers. The weights are more of a starting point for discussion than a final answer.

Note: Since the limits bind every quarter, I would have liked to also run the optimiser without the group limits to see what the limits actually cost in risk and return. I ran out of time for this, but it is the first thing I would add. I would also convert the global indices to rand once a USD/ZAR series is available.
